title: Can one expression give the bill for any order?
description: {{NAME_2}} buys a different order each time, at the same prices. Letters for the number of coconuts and the kilograms of jaggery give one expression for every bill, which is then used for eight coconuts and nine kilograms. Keeko doubts that the expression fits only the first order.
teaching_notes: One idea: letters for the changing amounts turn a bill into one expression, and putting numbers in place of the letters gives a particular bill. Watch for students who think the expression belongs to one order only.

source: Write an expression for the total to pay for c coconuts and j kg of jaggery, then use it for 8 coconuts and 9 kg of jaggery
video_script.why: A learner sees how the bill of one order becomes an expression with letters that fits every order.
video_script.substitution: The book's own prices, with c for the number of coconuts and j for the kilograms of jaggery, then eight coconuts and nine kilograms.
video_script.anchor: {{NAME_2}}'s laddu shop, buying coconuts and jaggery at fixed prices
video_script.wrong_answer: the expression is only for ten coconuts and five kilograms
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks the expression belongs to the first order, ten coconuts and five kilograms; the letters take any values, so it fits eight and nine as well.
video_script.payoff_line: {{NAME_2}} must pay eight hundred and twenty rupees

final_answer.spoken: the expression is c times thirty five plus j times sixty, and the bill is eight hundred and twenty rupees

never_show: the bill 820 before the answer beat
maths_rules: Cost of coconuts = c × 35. Cost of jaggery = j × 60.
Replace c by 8 and j by 9: 8 × 35 + 9 × 60 = 280 + 540 = 820 rupees.
video_script.design: One idea: letters for the changing amounts give one expression for every bill. Assumes the bill of a single order from the earlier example. The two price tags and the bill slip stay on the stage. Wrong idea: the expression fits one order only.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the coconut and the jaggery with their price tags; two order cards, one with a blank for the order

marks.p1: the title card From your book arrives
marks.p2: the price tags stay while two different order cards appear
marks.p3: a blank order card is shown with a question mark
marks.p4: the order of eight coconuts and nine kilograms is written on the second card

narration: <bookmark mark='p1'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='p2'/>{{NAME_2}} buys coconuts and jaggery at the same prices, but the order changes every time.
<bookmark mark='p3'/>The book asks for one expression that gives the bill for any order.
<bookmark mark='p4'/>It also asks for the bill when the order is eight coconuts and nine kilograms.
How can we write the expression?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a bill slip with a coconut line and a jaggery line; the numbers of items are blanks, the prices are fixed

marks.g1: the blanks for the number of coconuts and the kilograms of jaggery flash
marks.g2: the letters c and j are written in the blanks

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>On the bill, the number of coconuts and the kilograms of jaggery change with each order.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>We let c stand for the number of coconuts, and j for the kilograms of jaggery.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>The prices stay fixed, so they remain ordinary numbers.

beats.on_screen: Given: coconut 35 rupees each ; jaggery 60 rupees for 1 kg ; c coconuts and j kg

marks.gv2: c coconuts and j kg are written beside them

narration: <bookmark mark='gv1'/>Given, a coconut costs thirty five rupees, and one kilogram of jaggery costs sixty rupees.
<bookmark mark='gv2'/>The order is c coconuts and j kilograms of jaggery.

beats.on_screen: To find: an expression for the total cost ; the total for 8 coconuts and 9 kg

marks.fd2: the second aim is written under it

narration: <bookmark mark='fd1'/>We find an expression for the total cost of any order.
<bookmark mark='fd2'/>Then we use it for eight coconuts and nine kilograms.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: cost of coconuts = c × 35 ; cost of jaggery = j × 60

marks.s1a: the coconut line c × 35 is written
marks.s1b: the jaggery line j × 60 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>The cost of the coconuts is the number of coconuts times thirty five, so c times thirty five.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>The cost of the jaggery is j times sixty.

marks.s2a: the two costs are joined by a plus sign

narration: <bookmark mark='s2a'/>The total is the cost of the coconuts plus the cost of the jaggery.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>The expression is c times thirty five plus j times sixty.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: replace c by 8 and j by 9 ; 8 × 35 + 9 × 60

marks.s3a: c is replaced by 8 and j by 9

narration: <bookmark mark='s3a'/>For eight coconuts and nine kilograms, replace c by eight and j by nine.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>The expression becomes eight times thirty five plus nine times sixty.
<bookmark mark='s4a'/>Eight times thirty five is two hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='s4b'/>Nine times sixty is five hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='s4c'/>The bill is two hundred and eighty plus five hundred and forty.

marks.ans: 820 rupees is boxed beside the expression

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>{{NAME_2}} must pay eight hundred and twenty rupees.
The expression for any order is c times thirty five plus j times sixty.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: the expression is only for the first order, struck out; the expression is shown with 10 and 5, then 8 and 9, in the blanks

marks.d2: the expression is shown twice, once for each order

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Keeko thinks the expression is only for ten coconuts and five kilograms, the first order.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>But c and j are letter-numbers, so they can take any values we choose.
<bookmark mark='d3'/>Ten and five give one bill, eight and nine give another, and one expression covers both.
